- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. - general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

attachment.content:
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: I'll search for rate-limiting middleware in the codebase.

input.prompt:
Search this repository very thoroughly for any per-user API rate-limiting middleware. Look for:
1. Files or code referencing "rate limit", "rateLimit", "rate-limit", "throttle", "throttling"
2. Any middleware registration that enforces request limits per user
3. Any configuration of request limits (e.g., requests per minute/hour)

Search broadly across the entire codebase — check server code, middleware directories, API routes, configuration files, etc. Report every file and line where rate limiting is mentioned or configured.

content.text:
Here are the complete findings from my thorough search of the repository.

---

**This codebase does not contain any per-user API rate-limiting middleware.** There is no code anywhere in the repository that enforces request limits (per user, per IP, or globally) on API endpoints using a rate limiter, token bucket, sliding window, or any similar mechanism.

Here is what I found:

**1. No rate-limiting middleware exists**

I searched the entire codebase for:
- "rate limit", "rateLimit", "rate_limit", "rate-limit", "throttle", "throttling"
- HTTP 429 / `TooManyRequests` / `ResourceExhausted` (in a rate-limit context)
- Go rate-limiting libraries (`x/time/rate`, `httprate`, `tollbooth`, `ulule/limiter`, `didip/tollbooth`, `throttled`)
- Frontend rate-limiting packages (`express-rate-limit`, `bottleneck`, `p-throttle`)
- Configuration patterns like "requests per minute/hour/second", "max requests", "per user", "per IP"
- Any file named with "rate", "throttle", or "limiter" in the project source directories

None of the server middleware, Connect interceptors, or gRPC-Gateway middleware implement rate limiting. The registered middleware chain in `/bench/repo/server/server.go` (line 51-52) is limited to `middleware.Recover()` and a CORS middleware. The Connect interceptor chain in `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` (lines 132-138) consists of:
- `MetadataInterceptor` (header conversion)
- `LoggingInterceptor` (request logging)
- `RecoveryInterceptor` (panic recovery)
- `AuthInterceptor` (authentication/authorization)

No rate limiter is among them.

**2. The only mentions of "rate limit" are in documentation, not implementation**

- `/bench/repo/internal/email/doc.go` line 86: A comment saying `"Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse"` -- this is a security recommendation in a doc comment, not implemented code.
- `/bench/repo/internal/email/README.md` lines 286-297: A documentation section titled "Implement Rate Limiting" showing an example code snippet using `rate.NewLimiter(rate.Every(time.Second), 10)`. This is purely a recommendation for future work; the rate limiter is never actually instantiated or used.

**3. Concurrency limiting exists but is not per-user rate limiting**

The codebase uses semaphores to limit concurrent resource-intensive operations, but these are global concurrency caps, not per-user API rate limits:

- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` lines 39-41, 59-60: `thumbnailSemaphore` (max 3 concurrent) and `imageProcessingSemaphore` (max 2 concurrent).
- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/attachment_service.go` line 160: Returns `codes.ResourceExhausted` with message "too many image processing requests" when the image processing semaphore is full.
- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/attachment_service_image.go` lines 67-77: The `acquireImageProcessingSlot` function that acquires/releases the semaphore.
- `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` lines 45-46, 106-107, 447-451: Similar thumbnail semaphore (max 3 concurrent).

These semaphores do not track per-user usage or enforce time-windowed request limits.

**4. `golang.org/x/time` is an indirect dependency but is not used for rate limiting**

`/bench/repo/go.mod` line 151 lists `golang.org/x/time v0.15.0` as an indirect dependency (pulled in transitively by another package). It is never imported directly in any source file in the project for rate-limiting purposes.

**5. The scheduler middleware is unrelated**

`/bench/repo/internal/scheduler/middleware.go` defines middleware for a background job scheduler (Recovery, Logging, Timeout), not for HTTP/API rate limiting.

**Summary:** This repository has zero per-user API rate-limiting middleware. There are no request-per-minute/hour limits, no token bucket or sliding window implementations, no per-user or per-IP throttling, and no HTTP 429 responses for rate violations. The only related code is a documentation suggestion in the email package and global concurrency semaphores for image processing.
